title: Keto Beat Mediterranean and Low-Fat Diets on Liver Fat
hook: All three diets in the trial produced about 10% weight loss — but keto cut liver fat by 67% versus 45%, and about half the keto group no longer met the definition of prediabetes.
key_points: A clinical trial compared ketogenic, Mediterranean, and low-fat diets in people with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease.
All three groups lost roughly 10% of body weight — the diets tied on the scale.
Keto reduced liver fat by 67%, compared with about 45% for the other two diets.
About half the keto group no longer qualified as having prediabetes after four to five months.
The result suggests where you lose fat, not just how much, matters for metabolic health.
Keto is restrictive and hard to sustain — the best diet is still one you can actually keep.
content_html: Diet trials usually end in a tie, and in one sense this one did: people with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease lost about 10% of their body weight whether they were assigned a ketogenic, Mediterranean, or low-fat diet. The scale couldn't tell the diets apart. The liver could.
extra_html:
Keto reduced liver fat by 67%, against roughly 45% for the other two approaches, and about half the keto group no longer met the criteria for prediabetes after four to five months. That's the interesting part of the result: identical weight loss produced different metabolic outcomes, which suggests where the body sheds fat matters, not only how much it sheds. Fat stored in the liver is closely tied to insulin resistance, so clearing it out plausibly explains the prediabetes reversals.

The usual caution applies before anyone cuts carbs on the strength of a headline. This was a months-long trial in people who already had metabolic disease, not a general population, and ketogenic eating is restrictive enough that adherence over years is a real problem. The durable lesson is narrower and more useful: if you have fatty liver disease, the composition of the diet you lose weight on may matter — and that's a conversation to have with a clinician.

related.title: Reversing Prediabetes Pays Off for the Heart
related.hook: Prediabetes isn't a one-way street. People who brought their blood sugar back to normal cut their risk of dying from heart disease or being hospitalized for heart failure by 58%.

related.title: Coffee Tracks With a Markedly Healthier Liver
related.hook: Across 355,000 people followed 13 years, five-plus cups a day came with a 47% lower risk of liver cancer. Decaf worked too — so it isn't the caffeine doing the work.

related.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
related.hook: Type 2 diabetes often arrives slowly, with a warning stage called prediabetes — and at that stage, modest lifestyle changes can stop or delay it.

related.title: Weight Loss That Lasts
related.hook: Crash diets win the first month and lose the year. Slow, steady loss built on habits you can actually keep is what stays off.

flashcards.prompt: The three diets tied on weight loss. What separated keto?

choices.text: It cut liver fat by 67% versus about 45% for the others
Its participants lost twice as much body weight
It was the only diet participants stuck with

flashcards.explanation_html: All three groups lost about 10% of body weight. The difference showed up in liver fat — 67% reduction on keto versus roughly 45% — and in prediabetes status.

flashcards.prompt: What broader idea does this trial illustrate about weight loss?
flashcards.back_html: Where fat is lost matters, not just how much. Equal weight loss produced unequal metabolic results, with liver fat responding differently by diet.

flashcards.prompt: Why isn't this a blanket recommendation to go keto?
flashcards.back_html: The trial ran four to five months in people with obesity, prediabetes and fatty liver. Keto is restrictive and hard to sustain — a diet only helps for as long as you keep it.
